messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Non-binary
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 54

They are 46, South Asian, non-binary, and married, and when they first start describing what happened, they do it in a careful, measured way, as if keeping the words in a narrow corridor will keep everything else from spilling out. They work as a software engineer, a job that usually suits them: long stretches of focused thinking, predictable problems, quiet collaboration. Before the trauma, they liked the solidity of code, the sense that if something broke, it could be traced and fixed. They were the person who stayed late to solve the stubborn bug, then went home to cook with their spouse and talk about small things while music played in the kitchen.

The event that changes that rhythm happens on an ordinary evening, during a traffic stop that escalates with frightening speed. They are driving home alone after work when police pull them over. At first they assume it is a routine mistake, something that will resolve in a few minutes. Instead, they are ordered out of the car, told to keep their hands visible, told to stop asking questions. Their mind goes blank and hot at the same time. They remember the flash of a flashlight, the pressure of being pinned, the shock of hearing their own voice sound high and unfamiliar as they try to explain that they have done nothing wrong. What stays with them most is not a single blow but the total loss of control: the uniforms, the commands, the humiliation of being treated like a threat while they are trying to breathe and comply. Afterwards, there is soreness, bruising, and a long stretch of disbelief that this has really happened in a public street, in front of passing cars, under a sky that looked entirely ordinary.

In the days that follow, they do not sleep well. Each time they start to drift off, their body seems to brace again, as if expecting hands on their shoulders or the bark of an order. They replay the stop repeatedly, searching for the point where the outcome might have changed. At work, they can still function in a narrow sense, answering messages, reviewing code, sitting through meetings. But concentration now takes effort, and they find themselves reading the same line several times without taking it in. The screen can become strangely unreal, and they will suddenly notice that their jaw is clenched, their shoulders held rigid, their fingers cold. They begin avoiding errands that require driving after dark. The route home, once automatic, now feels charged with danger, every patrol car a trigger, every brake light a jolt through the chest.

Their spouse notices first how much they startle. A dropped pan, a sudden ringtone, even the click of a closing door can make them flinch before they can stop themselves. At home they become more watchful, checking locks, peering out windows, scanning the street before stepping outside. They do not like to be touched unexpectedly. Even affectionate contact can make their body jerk before their mind catches up. They try to hide this from their spouse, but the effort itself is exhausting, and sometimes it leaks out as irritability or flat silence. They hate that they seem angrier, less patient, less available. They also hate the shame that follows, especially because part of what the police did was leave them feeling publicly exposed and privately wronged in a way they cannot neatly explain.

Over time, they begin to carry a constant, low-level dread that something similar could happen again. News stories about police violence are impossible to ignore; they feel them in their stomach before they can even decide whether to keep reading. They avoid protests and demonstrations, even ones they once believed in deeply, because the idea of police presence now feels physically intolerable. They are not only afraid of being harmed again; they are afraid of being seen, singled out, misread. That fear reaches into ordinary life. If they are pulled behind schedule on the way to work, they feel panicky. If an unfamiliar car slows beside them, their heart races. Their body has become quick to anticipate attack, as though it has learned that safety is temporary and conditional.

When they speak about themselves now, there is often a split between the part that knows they are competent and the part that feels permanently diminished. They still write elegant code, still solve problems, still show up for their team. But there are mornings when getting dressed feels like assembling a version of themselves that no longer fits quite right. They sometimes sit in the parked car outside the office, hands on the steering wheel, trying to steady their breathing before going in. On those mornings, they think about how one encounter can alter the shape of a whole life, how a person can keep moving and working and loving while also carrying the constant knowledge that the world has become less safe than it once seemed.
